blocks.heading: What this section asks you to do
blocks.text: Define protection and its four methods, and explain how each method works at the border.

blocks.heading: Protection, and its four methods
blocks.text: Protection is government action that shelters home producers from import competition. The syllabus names four methods. A tariff is a tax on imported goods. An import quota is a limit on the quantity that may be imported in a period. A subsidy is a payment to home producers that lowers their costs. An embargo is a ban on trade with a country or in a product.

blocks.heading: How each method works
blocks.text: The four work differently. A tariff raises the import price at the border, so buyers who mind price tend to drift towards home goods, and the government collects the tax as revenue. A quota caps the quantity directly, whatever buyers would pay - no revenue reaches the government, and the shortage itself may push prices up. A subsidy lowers home producers' costs without touching the import, so home goods may price closer to it, with the cost landing on taxpayers instead of buyers. An embargo stops the trade entirely, and serves its purpose where home production or another supplier can fill the gap.

blocks.heading: The blanket tariff at Walvis Bay
blocks.text: Namibia places a tariff of N$50 on each imported blanket. The border price of an imported blanket rises from N$200 to N$250, since N$200 + N$50 = N$250. Over the following year imports fall from 8 000 blankets to 6 000, and the government collects 6 000 x N$50 = N$300 000 in revenue. Home blankets selling at N$230 now sit N$20 below the import, and home makers lift output from 3 000 blankets towards 3 800. Each number names who gains and who pays: buyers pay more, home producers sell more, the government collects revenue.

blocks.heading: A subsidy and an embargo at work
blocks.text:
Figures invented for teaching. Home boot makers in Keetmanshoop produce a pair at a cost of N$300 and need to charge N$320 to cover costs and earn a profit, while imported boots sell at N$280, so buyers tend to choose the import. The government pays home makers a subsidy of N$50 a pair. Their cost per pair falls to N$300 - N$50 = N$250, so they can charge N$270, below the imported price, and win back buyers. The import price is untouched and no tax is charged at the border; instead taxpayers pay N$50 for each pair made at home - 10 000 x N$50 = N$500 000 a year if the makers sell 10 000 pairs.

An embargo works by law, not price. If the government bans imports of a product, or all trade with one country - for example in a political dispute, or because goods are unsafe - none may enter, however low their price. Home producers and other suppliers fill the gap, but buyers lose that choice and, where few other suppliers exist, may pay much more.
